title: 3D-printed F-16 EDF jet
summary: A 50 mm EDF F-16 printed in lightweight PLA on a Bambu Lab P2S, from slicer tuning to wiring and radio setup.

photos.caption: Assembled, rear: EDF outlet and tailerons
Exploded view: every printed part and the electronics

specs.v: eSUN ePLA-LW (lightweight foaming PLA), PLA wing keys
RadioMaster Pocket (ExpressLRS) + BetaFPV ELRS 2.4G PWM receiver

milestones.text: Choose the airframe and buy the parts
Tune the slicer for lightweight PLA
Print test parts and compare settings
Rebuild the full 3D assembly in Blender
Solder the XT60 and wire the electronics
Bind the radio and calibrate the ESC
Glue up the airframe and fit the electronics
Check the centre of gravity and control throws

log.text: The PLA arrived. Sorted the STL files into a print queue (tail pods first as a test print) and set up Bambu Studio presets for eSUN ePLA-LW.

Switched to Troy McMillan's LW-PLA settings: 0.25 mm layers, a single wall, 3% gyroid / 6% grid infill and low flow so the foaming PLA expands into the gaps. Printed two tail pods side by side to compare against my first profile, then cut retraction and turned off z-hop to fight the stringing.

The kit has sockets for the wings but no joiner, so I measured the sockets in the STL files and designed two PLA wing keys with 0.3 mm and 0.5 mm clearance to test-print. Also rebuilt the whole jet as a 3D assembly in Blender to see what glues to what and where the electronics sit.
Rendered the assembly in Blender Cycles: studio lighting, metallic paint and an exploded view of every part.
Electronics: planned the wiring (battery → XT60 → ESC → EDF, servos and ESC into the receiver), set up the soldering iron, and started binding the RadioMaster Pocket to the ExpressLRS receiver.

body:
## The plan

A small, fast F-16 that I can print myself. The airframe is ptikyle's **"Built Fast" F-16 Gen 2**, printed in lightweight foaming PLA and powered by a **50 mm electric ducted fan** on a 4S battery. Everything is printed on my Bambu Lab P2S.

## Printing in lightweight PLA

LW-PLA foams as it prints, so it needs very different settings from normal PLA. What worked best for me (based on Troy McMillan's settings):

| Setting | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Layer height | 0.25 mm |
| Walls | 1 |
| Infill | 3% gyroid (6% grid on the tailerons) |
| Flow | 0.55 |
| Nozzle | 230 °C |
| Retraction | 0.2 mm, no z-hop |

The hardest part is stringing: LW-PLA leaves fine "hair" everywhere, so I'm still tuning retraction and travel.

## Wing joiner keys

The wings plug into stubs on the fuselage, but there was no file for the part that joins them. I measured the sockets from the STL files (a slanted 22 × 11 mm tunnel in the fuselage and a 13 × 3 mm pocket in each wing) and designed a key in two fits, standard (0.3 mm) and loose (0.5 mm), to test which one slides in best.

## 3D assembly

To understand how the 17 printed parts fit together, I rebuilt the whole jet as an assembly in Blender, with an exploded view, the electronics in the equipment bay and the wire routes.

## Electronics

The 4S battery feeds a 40 A ESC through an XT60 plug. The ESC drives the EDF and powers the receiver and servos through its built-in BEC. Two MG90S servos move the tailerons, mixed on the radio as elevons so they handle both pitch and roll.

## What's next

Finish printing, solder the power leads, set up the radio mixes and calibrate the ESC. Then glue up, balance and fly.
